header: AUN-INI-105 -- INI MCQ .pdf, Chapter 2 "Bacterial growth" (pp.28-37, 60 items, plain-text ANSWERS table p37; coverage/AUN-INI-105-triage.md's chapter map). This batch authors the 12 of 60 questions whose tested idea rides on a newly-minted AUN-INI-105 concept (concept/AUN-INI-105-ch2-concepts.md, article/AUN-INI-105-ch2-article.md): the definition of bacterial growth, binary fission as the reproductive mechanism, the growth-curve/disease-stage correlation, and aerotolerant anaerobes. The remaining 40 keyed questions reuse eight pending Ain-Shams ASU-INF-microbiology-concepts.md concepts (plus the already-overlaid mesosome concept) and are authored separately in pending-live/ with an apply-after header. Eight items are held: Q20 (figure-dependent, no extractable diagram), Q42 (printed key conflicts with the expected answer), and six near-verbatim duplicates of other chapter-2 items (Q28, Q31, Q37, Q56, Q58, Q60).

questions.title: Definition of bacterial growth
questions.question: The orderly increase in all components of protoplasm of a cell is called?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Reproduction describes the production of new daughter cells (in bacteria, via binary fission); it names the outcome event, not the orderly, proportional increase of a cell's own protoplasmic components that precedes it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cell division is the physical splitting of one cell into two; it is the mechanism that converts individual-cell growth into population increase, not the definition of growth itself.
explanations.C: Correct. "Growth" specifically names the orderly increase in all of a cell's protoplasmic components -- its cytoplasm, membranes, ribosomes and other constituents increasing together in proportion -- rather than any single event such as division. This proportional, whole-cell increase is what must happen before a bacterium is large enough to divide, making growth logically prior to, and distinct from, reproduction and cell division.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Reproduction and cell division are each a specific event distinct from the protoplasmic increase that defines growth, so "all of the above" incorrectly collapses growth into its own downstream consequences.

questions.learning_objective: Define bacterial growth as the orderly increase in all of a cell's protoplasmic components, distinct from reproduction or cell division as isolated events.

questions.title: Bacterial cell multiplication: usual mechanism
questions.question: The bacterial cell multiplication is usually by?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mitosis is a eukaryotic process using a mitotic spindle to segregate paired chromosomes; bacteria have no nucleus or spindle apparatus and do not divide by mitosis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Meiosis is the eukaryotic reductive division that halves chromosome number to form gametes; bacteria are haploid with a single chromosome and have no meiotic cycle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Conjugation is a mechanism of horizontal gene transfer between two bacterial cells via a sex pilus; it moves genetic material between existing cells but is not itself how a bacterial cell multiplies.
explanations.D: Correct. Bacterial cells usually multiply by binary fission: a single cell replicates its chromosome and splits into two genetically identical daughter cells. This simple, asexual mechanism -- not mitosis, meiosis or conjugation -- is the ordinary route of bacterial multiplication, and it is what the bacterial growth curve actually tracks over time.

questions.learning_objective: Identify binary fission as the usual mechanism of bacterial cell multiplication, distinct from the eukaryotic processes of mitosis and meiosis and from conjugation.

field_notes.keySource: printed plain-text ANSWERS table, chapter 2, p37

questions.title: Bacteria multiply by simple binary fission
questions.question: Bacteria multiply by?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Spore formation (sporulation) is a survival strategy certain Gram-positive genera use under nutrient-poor or hostile conditions, producing a dormant endospore -- it is not the ordinary route by which a bacterial population multiplies.
explanations.B: Correct. Bacteria multiply by simple binary fission: one cell duplicates its single chromosome and divides into two identical daughter cells, without any spore, sexual, or gamete-based step. This asexual mechanism is what produces the exponential increase in cell number seen during the log phase of the growth curve.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Conjugation transfers genetic material (often a plasmid) from a donor to a recipient bacterial cell across a pilus; it changes a recipient's genetic content but does not itself produce a new daughter cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gametes are haploid sex cells produced by eukaryotic meiosis for sexual reproduction; bacteria have no gametes and do not reproduce sexually.

questions.learning_objective: State that bacteria multiply by simple binary fission, distinct from spore formation, conjugation, and gamete-based sexual reproduction.

questions.title: Convalescence corresponds to the decline phase
questions.question: Convalescence stage of the disease is corresponding to?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lag phase, when bacteria are adapting to a new environment with no net division, corresponds instead to the incubation period of disease -- before symptoms appear, not to recovery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The logarithmic (exponential) phase, when division is at its maximum rate, corresponds to the invasive period of disease, as the organism spreads and symptoms escalate -- the opposite direction from convalescence.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The stationary phase, when new cells balance dying cells and the population plateaus, corresponds to the period of overt symptoms and signs -- the clinical peak of illness, not its resolution.
explanations.D: Correct. Convalescence is the recovery stage of an infectious disease, when the pathogen population is falling as host defences and/or treatment take effect. This maps onto the decline (death) phase of the bacterial growth curve, in which dying cells outnumber newly formed ones and the population shrinks -- the direct in-vitro counterpart of a patient's clinical recovery.

questions.subtopic: Growth curve correlation with disease stages
questions.learning_objective: State that the decline phase of the bacterial growth curve corresponds to the convalescence (recovery) stage of infectious disease, distinct from the lag, log and stationary phases' own disease correlates.

questions.title: Lag phase correlates with the incubation period
questions.question: The lag phase of bacterial growth curve correlate in vivo with which of the following?

options.E: Marker of chronic phase of the disease

explanations.A: Incorrect. Overt symptoms and signs correspond instead to the stationary phase, the clinical peak of illness, once the organism's population has already expanded -- not to the lag phase, before division has even begun.
explanations.B: Correct. The lag phase is the period during which bacteria adapt to a new environment and accumulate the enzymes needed for multiplication, with no net cell division yet occurring. This silent adaptation period is the direct in-vitro counterpart of the incubation period in vivo -- the interval after infection during which the pathogen establishes itself before any symptoms appear.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The invasive period, when the organism is actively spreading and symptoms are escalating, corresponds to the exponential (log) phase of maximal division, not the lag phase.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Convalescence (recovery) corresponds to the decline phase, when the pathogen population is falling -- the opposite end of the disease course from the lag phase's silent establishment.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Marker of chronic phase of the disease" is not a recognised correlate in this four-phase growth-curve-to-disease-stage scheme; the lag phase's specific correlate is the incubation period.

questions.subtopic: Growth curve correlation with disease stages
questions.learning_objective: State that the lag phase of the bacterial growth curve corresponds to the incubation period of infectious disease.

questions.title: Stationary phase correlates with symptoms and signs
questions.question: Which one of the following is correct for stationary phase of bacterial growth?

options.A: Correlates with symptoms & signs in vivo
options.B: The division occurs at maximum & constant rate
options.C: The rate of division depends on the nature of the organism
options.D: It continues until nutrients in the medium become exhausted
options.E: Correlates with invasive period in vivo

explanations.A: Correct. The stationary phase, when the number of newly formed cells balances the number of dying cells and the population plateaus at its peak, corresponds in vivo to the period of overt symptoms and signs -- the clinical peak of an infection, once the organism has already reached its maximum burden. This is the point at which a patient's illness is typically most apparent, since the pathogen load driving those symptoms is at its highest and steadiest.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Division at its maximum and constant rate describes the exponential (log) phase, not the stationary phase, in which net division has instead fallen to zero as births and deaths balance.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The nature of the organism is a determinant more specifically associated with the length of the lag phase, not a defining feature of the stationary phase itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nutrient exhaustion is what drives the population INTO the stationary phase (and later the decline phase) rather than something the stationary phase itself continues until; by the time stationary phase is established, nutrients are already limiting.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The invasive period corresponds instead to the exponential (log) phase, when the organism is actively multiplying and spreading -- not to the stationary phase's clinical-peak correlate.

questions.subtopic: Growth curve correlation with disease stages
questions.learning_objective: State that the stationary phase of the bacterial growth curve corresponds to overt symptoms and signs in vivo, not to maximal division rate, lag-phase determinants, or the invasive period.

questions.title: Binary fission relies on a single chromosome
questions.question: Reproduction in bacterin takes place by binary fission as they possess?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Multiple chromosomes would require a more complex segregation mechanism (as eukaryotic mitosis has); a bacterium's simple binary fission relies instead on a single genome copy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Spores are dormant survival structures formed by certain Gram-positive genera under stress, not the genetic basis that enables ordinary binary fission.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A bacterial chromosome is typically circular, not linear; a linear chromosome is not the feature that enables simple binary fission here.
explanations.D: Correct. Bacteria typically carry a single, usually circular, chromosome. Having only one chromosome to replicate and segregate -- rather than multiple paired chromosomes needing a mitotic spindle -- is exactly what makes simple binary fission possible: one replication event, one segregation, one division into two identical daughters.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Bacteria lack a nucleolus entirely (they lack a true nucleus altogether), but the absence of a nucleolus is not itself the feature that enables binary fission; the enabling feature is the single chromosome.

questions.learning_objective: State that a bacterium's single (usually circular) chromosome is what makes its simple binary fission mechanism possible.

questions.title: Invasion period corresponds to the logarithmic phase
questions.question: The invasion period in vivo is corresponding in vitro to?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lag phase, with no net division occurring, corresponds instead to the silent incubation period before symptoms appear, not to the actively spreading invasion period.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The stationary phase, a plateau in cell number, corresponds to the clinical peak of overt symptoms and signs, which follows invasion rather than describing it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The decline phase, when the population is falling, corresponds to convalescence/recovery -- the opposite end of the disease course from active invasion.
explanations.D: Correct. The logarithmic (exponential) phase is when bacterial division occurs at its maximal rate, and this rapid in-vitro multiplication is the direct counterpart of the invasive period in vivo, during which the pathogen actively spreads through the host and symptoms escalate. This is also, for the same reason, the phase during which cell-wall-active antibiotics are most effective, since dividing cells present the most targets for disruption.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Retardation phase" (a brief slowing transition sometimes described between exponential and stationary phases) is not the phase named for the invasive period in this scheme; that correlate is the logarithmic phase itself.

questions.subtopic: Growth curve correlation with disease stages
questions.learning_objective: State that the logarithmic (exponential) phase of the bacterial growth curve corresponds to the invasive period of infectious disease.

questions.title: Recovery corresponds to the decline phase
questions.question: The recovery stage in vivo is?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lag phase corresponds to the incubation period, before symptoms even appear -- the start of the disease course, not its recovery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The stationary phase corresponds to the clinical peak of symptoms and signs, when the pathogen burden is at its highest, not to recovery.
explanations.C: Correct. Recovery -- convalescence -- is the stage during which host defences and/or treatment cause the pathogen population to fall. This corresponds to the decline (death) phase of the bacterial growth curve, in which dying cells outnumber newly formed ones and the total population shrinks, the direct in-vitro counterpart of a patient's recovery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The logarithmic phase, division at its maximal rate, corresponds to the invasive period, when the disease is worsening -- the opposite direction from recovery.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Retardation phase" is not the correlate named for recovery in this scheme; recovery's counterpart is specifically the decline phase.

questions.subtopic: Growth curve correlation with disease stages
questions.learning_objective: State that the decline phase of the bacterial growth curve corresponds to the recovery stage of infectious disease.

questions.title: Aerotolerant anaerobes are not killed by oxygen exposure
questions.question: Anaerobes that are not Killed by exposure to oxygen are?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Obligate anaerobes are, by definition, the group that IS killed or fails to grow on exposure to oxygen, because they lack the enzymes (catalase, superoxide dismutase) needed to detoxify the reactive oxygen species oxygen exposure generates -- the opposite of the organisms this question describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Microaerophilic bacteria grow best with only small (trace) amounts of oxygen and are, like obligate anaerobes, harmed by full atmospheric oxygen concentrations; that is a preference/tolerance issue distinct from the aerotolerant anaerobe's outright survival of oxygen exposure.
explanations.C: Correct. Aerotolerant anaerobes do not use oxygen in their metabolism at all -- like obligate anaerobes, they rely on fermentative, anaerobic pathways -- but unlike obligate anaerobes they are not killed by oxygen's presence. This tolerance is generally attributed to their retaining enough superoxide dismutase and/or peroxidase to detoxify incidental reactive oxygen species, even without using oxygen for energy production.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Thermophilic describes temperature preference (bacteria that grow best at high temperatures), an entirely different environmental axis from oxygen tolerance.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Autotrophic describes carbon-source use (synthesising organic compounds from inorganic CO2), an entirely different classification axis from oxygen tolerance.

questions.learning_objective: Identify aerotolerant anaerobes as organisms that do not use oxygen metabolically but, unlike obligate anaerobes, are not killed by its presence.

questions.title: Bacterial cell multiplies by binary fission
questions.question: Bacterial cell multiplies by?

explanations.A: Correct. A bacterial cell multiplies by binary fission -- replicating its single chromosome and splitting into two identical daughter cells. This simple asexual mechanism, not budding, sexual multiplication or mitosis, is the ordinary route of bacterial reproduction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Budding is a reproductive strategy seen in some yeasts and a small number of bacteria (e.g. Hyphomicrobium) in which a smaller daughter cell forms as an outgrowth of the parent; it is not the usual bacterial reproductive mechanism being tested here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sexual multiplication implies gamete fusion and genetic recombination between two parents producing offspring; bacteria reproduce asexually by binary fission, though they can separately exchange genes by conjugation, transformation or transduction, which are not reproduction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mitosis is a eukaryotic process requiring a mitotic spindle to segregate paired chromosomes; bacteria, lacking a nucleus and spindle apparatus, do not divide by mitosis.

questions.learning_objective: State that a bacterial cell multiplies by binary fission, distinct from budding, sexual multiplication and mitosis.

questions.title: Growth of bacteria: increase in size and number
questions.question: Growth of bacteria refers to?

explanations.A: Incorrect alone (true but partial). An individual bacterial cell does increase in size as it grows, but this is only one facet of what "growth of bacteria" as a population-level term refers to, not the complete answer.
explanations.B: Incorrect alone (true but partial). A bacterial population does increase in cell number through repeated binary fission, but this too is only one facet, not the complete answer by itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Deposition of fat (as an intracellular storage inclusion) is not what defines bacterial growth; it is an unrelated metabolic storage phenomenon, not a growth criterion.
explanations.D: Correct. "Growth of bacteria" refers jointly to an increase in cell size and an increase in cell number -- at the individual-cell level a cell grows in size before dividing, and at the population level growth is observed as an increase in the number of cells. Since both A and B are genuine facets of bacterial growth and C is not, "A,B" is the accurate combined answer rather than either alone or "all of the above." This combined size-and-number framing is why the growth curve, which plots cell number, is only one lens on bacterial growth -- individual cells also enlarge before each division.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "All of the above" would wrongly include deposition of fat (C) as a defining feature of growth, when fat deposition is an unrelated storage phenomenon, not a growth criterion.

questions.learning_objective: State that bacterial growth refers jointly to an increase in cell size and an increase in cell number, not to fat deposition.
